title: “EVERYONE DID WHAT WAS RIGHT IN HIS OWN EYES”—THE BIBLE’S CIVIL WAR THAT ENDED WITH A SENTENCE MORE TERRIFYING THAN THE BLOODSHED
paragraphs: “EVERYONE DID WHAT WAS RIGHT IN HIS OWN EYES”—THE BIBLE’S CIVIL WAR THAT ENDED WITH A SENTENCE MORE TERRIFYING THAN THE BLOODSHED
When an entire nation called its own desires righteousness, the innocent paid the price. And the final verse of Judges exposes a danger that still lives inside the human heart today.
There is a sentence in the Bible that should make every Christian uncomfortable.
Not because it describes a demon.
Not because it announces a plague.
Not even because it speaks of an invading army.
But because it describes ordinary people who had become so convinced of their own righteousness that they could no longer recognize how far they had wandered from God.

And by the time that sentence appeared, a woman had been brutally abused and killed, a nation had descended into civil war, tens of thousands had died, cities had been destroyed, and hundreds of women had been treated as possessions to solve a political crisis.
The people responsible were not strangers to the name of God.
They were Israel.
The covenant people.
The people who had witnessed divine deliverance, received God's commandments, and inherited a land they could never have conquered without His mercy.
And yet the book of Judges closes with these chilling words:
“In those days there was no king in Israel: every man did that which was right in his own eyes.” — Judges 21:25, KJV
Read that again.
Not everyone did what they knew was evil.
Everyone did what was right in his own eyes.
That is what makes this verse so frightening.
Because the most dangerous spiritual blindness is not always the person who knows he is rebelling against God.
Sometimes it is the person who has convinced himself that God agrees with him.
And before we condemn ancient Israel, there is a question we must be brave enough to ask.
What if the same sentence could be written about us?
What if we have become so accustomed to defending our choices, excusing our compromises, and protecting our reputations that we have forgotten how to tremble before the Word of God?
What if the greatest danger to our souls is not that we have stopped believing in God, but that we have started believing our own opinions are as authoritative as His voice?
Stay with this story.
Because its ending is not merely about a nation that lost its way.
It is about the kind of Savior a lost world desperately needs.
And perhaps, somewhere in the ruins of this ancient tragedy, you will recognize something you have been trying not to see in yourself.
The Hebrew of Judges 21:25 reads:
בַּיָּמִים הָהֵם אֵין מֶלֶךְ בְּיִשְׂרָאֵל אִישׁ הַיָּשָׁר בְּעֵינָיו יַעֲשֶׂה
Bayyamim hahem ein melekh beYisra'el; ish hayyashar be'enav ya'aseh.
A close translation is:
“In those days there was no king in Israel; each person would do what was right in his own eyes.”
The word הַיָּשָׁר (hayyashar) comes from a Hebrew root associated with what is straight, upright, or right.
The expression בְּעֵינָיו (be'enav) means “in his eyes.”
And the closing verb, יַעֲשֶׂה (ya'aseh), expresses the action of doing.
Notice the contrast.
The issue is not simply that people acted.
It is that their own perception had become the standard by which their actions were judged.
Their eyes had become their courtroom.
Their desires had become their witnesses.
Their opinions had become their verdict.
But Scripture had already warned Israel against this very condition.
Deuteronomy 12:8 says:
“Ye shall not do after all the things that we do here this day, every man whatsoever is right in his own eyes.”
The tragedy of Judges is that Israel eventually became the very people God had warned them not to become.
And it did not happen overnight.
Spiritual collapse rarely does.
It happens when one compromise becomes acceptable.
When one act of disobedience is explained away.
When one generation stops teaching the next generation why God's commands matter.
When worship becomes a cultural identity instead of a surrendered life.
When people still speak God's name but increasingly refuse His authority.
Judges 2:10 describes a generation that arose after Joshua, one that did not know the LORD or the works He had done for Israel.
That does not necessarily mean every person had never heard God's name.
It reveals a devastating failure of covenant faithfulness and spiritual continuity.
The stories of God's mighty works had not produced a faithful generation.
And by the closing chapters of Judges, the consequences were horrifying.
In Judges 19, a Levite traveled with his concubine, a woman whose status in that ancient society left her especially vulnerable.
They arrived in Gibeah, a town belonging to Benjamin, one of Israel's own tribes.
What happened that night should never be softened into a comfortable religious illustration.
A mob surrounded the house where they were staying and demanded that the male guest be brought outside for sexual abuse.
The host proposed offering women instead.
Eventually, the Levite sent his concubine outside.
She was sexually assaulted through the night.
At daybreak, she collapsed at the doorway.
The text then describes the Levite finding her, placing her on his donkey, and taking her home. He subsequently dismembered her body into twelve pieces and sent them throughout Israel.
Judges 19 does not explicitly establish the precise moment of her death, but the account presents an appalling sequence of violence, betrayal, and dehumanization.
And here is something that must not be overlooked.
The Bible records what happened.
It does not command us to admire what happened.
The narrative exposes the moral disintegration of Israel. It does not present the Levite, the host, or the attackers as models of godly conduct.
The woman had almost no voice in the story.
Men made decisions.
Men defended their honor.
Men invoked the outrage of the nation.
And a woman bore the consequences of their wickedness.
That should trouble us.
Because whenever human beings become more concerned about preserving their image than protecting the vulnerable, something has gone terribly wrong.
And whenever religion is used to excuse cruelty, we are not witnessing holiness.
We are witnessing the corruption of something sacred.
The Levite's gruesome message stirred the tribes of Israel.
They assembled and demanded justice.
Benjamin refused to surrender the guilty men of Gibeah.
And what began as a demand for accountability became a civil war.
Brother fought brother.
Israelite fought Israelite.
The nation that should have stood united in covenant faithfulness turned its weapons against itself.

Judges 20 records catastrophic losses. Tens of thousands of fighting men died, including approximately forty thousand Israelites in the first two days of battle and twenty-five thousand Benjamite warriors in the subsequent defeat.
The victorious Israelites then attacked Benjamite towns, killing inhabitants and livestock and burning cities.
Only six hundred Benjamite men escaped to the rock of Rimmon.
Imagine the silence afterward.
Homes without fathers.
Families without sons.
Cities reduced to ashes.
A people who had sought to confront wickedness now standing amid the devastation of their own nation.
And then came another tragedy.
Israel realized that Benjamin, one of the twelve tribes, was facing near extinction.
But the Israelites had previously sworn not to give their daughters in marriage to Benjamite men.
Instead of humbly confronting the disastrous consequences of their decisions, they searched for a way around their oath.
They attacked Jabesh-gilead because its inhabitants had not attended the national assembly, and they brought back four hundred young women for the surviving Benjamites.
When that was not enough, they instructed the remaining men to seize young women during a festival at Shiloh.
Read Judges 21:10–23 for yourself.
It is disturbing.
And it is meant to be disturbing.
The chapter shows a community so entangled in violence, rash vows, and moral confusion that its proposed solutions perpetuated the suffering of innocent people.
The narrative does not portray the seizure of women as God's ideal for marriage.
It reveals how deeply the nation's judgment had deteriorated.
And after all of it—after the abuse, the murder, the civil war, the slaughter, and the abductions—the book ends.
No triumphant celebration.
No comforting declaration that everything had finally been repaired.
Just that terrible diagnosis.
“Every man did that which was right in his own eyes.”
The sentence lands like a door closing on a darkened room.
And now comes the uncomfortable part.
Because we cannot read Judges faithfully if we only point at the ancient Israelites and say, “How could they?”
We must also ask, “Lord, where have I begun to resemble them?”
Perhaps you have never committed the terrible acts described in these chapters.
But have you ever defended something simply because admitting you were wrong would cost you your pride?
Have you ever hurt someone and spent more time explaining your intentions than acknowledging their pain?
Have you ever called something a blessing because you wanted it badly, even while knowing it required disobedience?
Have you ever used a Bible verse to win an argument while refusing to let that same Bible correct your heart?
Have you ever asked God to approve a decision you had already made?
That last question may be the one that hurts.
Because sometimes we do not actually want God's guidance.
We want His endorsement.
We want heaven to sign beneath choices our flesh has already approved.
And when Scripture challenges us, we become defensive.
When a faithful friend corrects us, we become offended.
When conviction interrupts our plans, we call it negativity.
We begin to confuse peace with comfort, freedom with self-rule, and grace with permission.
But grace was never given to make rebellion feel safe.
Titus 2:11–12 teaches that the grace of God brings salvation and trains believers to reject ungodliness and live righteous, godly lives.
Real grace does not merely comfort us while we remain enslaved to sin.
It teaches us to turn away from what is destroying us.
This is why the repeated statement about Israel having no king matters so much.
Judges 17:6, 18:1, 19:1, and 21:25 all draw attention to the absence of a king.
In its historical and literary setting, this refrain points toward Israel's need for righteous leadership and prepares readers for the monarchy that follows in the biblical story.
But we must be careful.
The Bible does not teach that simply placing a human king on a throne would cure the human heart.
Israel would eventually have kings.
Some would lead faithfully.
Many would lead the people into even greater wickedness.
And in 1 Samuel 8:7, when Israel demanded a king like the surrounding nations, the LORD told Samuel that the people had rejected Him from reigning over them.
So the deepest problem was never merely the absence of a political ruler.
It was the absence of faithful submission to the LORD.
And that is where this dark story begins pointing us toward something greater.
Someone greater.
A King who would not exploit the vulnerable.
A King who would not preserve His reputation by sacrificing the innocent.
A King who would not demand that others bleed to protect His pride.
A King who would come into a broken world and willingly shed His own blood to redeem sinners.
Jesus Christ.
Think about the contrast.
In Judges 19, a vulnerable woman is handed over to violent men while those responsible for her protection fail her.
In the Gospel, Jesus willingly gives Himself for His people.
The first is a horrifying act of human betrayal.
The second is the voluntary, saving sacrifice of the sinless Son of God.
They are not morally equivalent events.
And Scripture does not explicitly identify the woman in Judges 19 as a prophetic symbol of Christ.
But reading these passages together reveals a profound moral contrast between sinful human leadership and the self-giving love of the true King.
Jesus says in John 10:11:
“I am the good shepherd: the good shepherd giveth his life for the sheep.”
Human sin abandons the vulnerable.
The Good Shepherd lays down His life.
Human pride sacrifices others to preserve itself.
Christ humbles Himself in obedience to the Father, even unto death on the cross.
Human kingdoms are stained by the failures of their rulers.
Christ's kingdom rests upon the righteousness of a King who never sinned.
And suddenly the question becomes more personal than political.
Who is ruling your heart?
Not whose name appears in your social media biography.
Not what denomination you attend.
Who actually has the final authority when God's Word contradicts what you want?
Because it is possible to call Jesus “Lord” while resisting His lordship.
Jesus Himself asked in Luke 6:46:
“And why call ye me, Lord, Lord, and do not the things which I say?”
That question has not lost its power.
It still reaches into our marriages.
Our private conversations.
Our finances.
Our sexual choices.
Our resentments.
Our hidden habits.
Our treatment of people who cannot repay us.
Our willingness to tell the truth when lying would be easier.
Our response when someone exposes our wrongdoing.
And perhaps the most revealing place of all: the secret life no one sees.
Because the real test of surrender is often what we choose when nobody is watching.
You may have spent years building a Christian appearance while quietly protecting something Christ has been calling you to surrender.
A relationship you know is pulling you away from obedience.
A bitterness you have rehearsed so often that it now feels like justice.
A secret habit you keep promising to abandon tomorrow.
An apology you refuse to make because you believe the other person should apologize first.
A pattern of dishonesty you have renamed survival.
A form of pride you have mistaken for strength.
And maybe this article is uncomfortable because you recognize the pattern.
Not the atrocities of Judges.
But the instinct beneath them.
The instinct to place ourselves at the center of moral authority.
To say, “I know what God says, but in my situation…”
And then finish the sentence with whatever we have already decided to do.
Friend, that is a dangerous place to live.
Not because Jesus is unwilling to forgive you.
But because self-deception can make a person unwilling to seek forgiveness.
The greatest danger is not discovering that you have sinned.
The greatest danger is becoming so committed to defending your sin that you no longer want to be rescued from it.
Yet this is where the Gospel becomes breathtaking.
Because Jesus did not enter the world to save people who had successfully made themselves righteous.
He came to save sinners.
Romans 5:8 declares:
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.”
While we were yet sinners.
Not after we cleaned up every hidden failure.
Not after we repaired every damaged relationship.
Not after we finally became impressive enough for heaven.
Christ died for sinners.
And His resurrection declares that death and sin do not have the final word over those who belong to Him.
But do not misunderstand this mercy.
Forgiveness is not a license to continue destroying yourself and others.
Repentance is not merely feeling bad because you were exposed.
It is turning toward God, acknowledging sin for what it is, and entrusting yourself to Jesus Christ.
The Greek New Testament uses the word μετάνοια (metanoia) for repentance, a term associated with a change of mind and, in biblical context, a turning toward God that bears fruit in life.
It is not merely emotional regret.
It is a reorientation of the person before God.
And the Greek word χάρις (charis), commonly translated “grace,” reminds us that salvation is God's undeserved favor, not a reward we purchase through religious performance.
Ephesians 2:8–9 says:
“For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God: Not of works, lest any man should boast.”
That is why your darkest chapter does not have to be your final chapter.
Not because your sin was small.
Not because your excuses were convincing.
Not because your good deeds outweighed your failures.
But because Jesus Christ is mighty to save.
And there is a beautiful contrast between the final verse of Judges and the message of the Gospel.
Judges ends with everyone doing what was right in their own eyes.
Jesus calls His disciples to deny themselves, take up their cross, and follow Him.
The first way enthrones the self.
The second submits the self to Christ.
The first asks, “What seems right to me?”
The second asks, “Lord, what would You have me do?”
The first protects pride.
The second learns humility.
The first can leave wounded people behind while claiming righteousness.
The second calls us to love our neighbors, seek justice, show mercy, and walk faithfully before God.
And none of that means Christians become perfect overnight.
We still struggle.
We still need correction.
We still confess.
We still depend upon mercy.
But the direction of our lives changes because the One who saved us is also the One who leads us.
Perhaps you are reading this after making a decision you deeply regret.
Perhaps someone trusted you, and you betrayed that trust.
Perhaps you have been hiding behind spiritual language while knowing that something in your life is terribly wrong.
Perhaps you are not the person who caused the harm.
Perhaps you are the one who was harmed.
Then hear this carefully.
The atrocities recorded in Judges do not mean God approves of abuse, coercion, or the destruction of vulnerable people.
And if someone has used religion to pressure you into silence about abuse, that misuse of Scripture does not represent the heart of Jesus Christ.
Seeking safety, telling the truth, and obtaining appropriate help are not betrayals of faith.
The God who sees what human beings conceal is not fooled by religious appearances.
And the Gospel never requires victims to pretend that evil was good.
Christ calls sinners to repentance.
He also calls His people to defend the vulnerable and practice justice.
Isaiah 1:17 says:
“Learn to do well; seek judgment, relieve the oppressed, judge the fatherless, plead for the widow.”
Biblical holiness is not measured by how loudly we condemn the world while ignoring the wounded at our doorstep.
It is revealed in obedience to God, including how we treat people who have no power to defend themselves.
That is one of the reasons this ancient story still matters.
It forces us to confront the possibility that religious communities can become deeply corrupted when loyalty to a group replaces loyalty to truth.
When protecting an institution matters more than protecting people.
When a leader's reputation becomes more important than repentance.
When a community calls accountability persecution.
When we condemn the sins of outsiders while making excuses for the sins of our own.
And when we begin to believe that being on the right side of an argument automatically means our hearts are right before God.
Judges refuses to let us become comfortable with that illusion.
It shows us a nation where people could recognize wickedness in others while repeatedly failing to confront the disorder within themselves.
Does that sound painfully familiar?
Maybe the verse that closes Judges is not merely describing ancient Israel.
Maybe it is holding up a mirror.
And perhaps the most merciful thing God can do for us today is allow that mirror to expose what we would rather keep hidden.
Because what is exposed can be confessed.
What is confessed can be brought before Christ.
And what is surrendered to Him can become the beginning of a changed life.
First John 1:9 gives this promise:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”
Not some unrighteousness.
All unrighteousness.
That does not erase earthly consequences or remove our responsibility to make things right where possible.
But it means guilt does not have to become your permanent identity.
Shame does not have to become your master.
Your past does not have to become the throne from which your future is ruled.
Jesus Christ is a better King.
And He does not merely offer better advice.
He offers redemption.
So perhaps tonight you need to stop explaining.
Stop rehearsing the reasons.
Stop comparing your sin to someone else's.
Stop saying, “At least I am not as bad as…”
And simply come before God.
No performance.
No religious mask.
No carefully edited testimony.
Just the truth.

“Lord Jesus, I have been doing what was right in my own eyes. I have defended what You were calling me to surrender. Forgive me. Change my heart. Teach me to love what You love and turn away from what dishonors You. I cannot save myself. I trust in Your death and resurrection. Be Lord over the parts of my life I have tried to keep for myself. Amen.”
You do not need to make that prayer impressive.
You need to mean what you say.
And if you have already trusted Christ but have wandered into compromise, return to Him.
Do not let yesterday's failure become tomorrow's excuse.
Repentance is not the enemy of joy.
It is the path back toward fellowship with the God whose mercy you need.
There is one more thing I want you to consider.
Someone in your life may be living through a spiritual civil war right now.
Outwardly, they look fine.
They go to work.
They laugh in photographs.
They answer messages.
They post Scripture.
But inside, they are exhausted from trying to rule a life they were never meant to rule apart from God.
They know something is wrong.
They just do not know how to come home.
Perhaps this article could become the beginning of a conversation they have been afraid to start.
Not because it is comfortable.
But because there may come a day when you need to read Judges 21:25 again and remember that sincerity alone does not make a choice righteous.
God's Word must correct our eyes.
Where has God been teaching you to surrender your own understanding and trust His Word?
Maybe your answer is “I am still fighting.”
Maybe it is “Pray for me.”
Maybe it is “Jesus, forgive me.”
Or perhaps you have a testimony of how Christ brought you out of a season when you insisted on doing everything your own way.
You do not have to disclose private wounds or details you are not ready to share.
But your honest words may encourage another believer who thought they were struggling alone.
Not as a formula for receiving salvation.
Not as a public performance.
But as a simple expression of the surrender you desire to live.
Because the Christian life was never meant to be sustained by one emotional moment.
We need the Word.
We need prayer.
We need sound teaching.
We need fellowship and accountability.
We need to keep returning to the cross and remembering whose righteousness saves us.
That is the heart behind Gospel Warrior.
Not merely producing content people will read today and forget tomorrow, but helping people encounter biblical truth that calls them toward lasting discipleship in Jesus Christ.
You glorify God through faith in Christ and a life of loving obedience—not by purchasing access to a ministry.
Those resources and products are not the reason we proclaim Christ.
Your prayers matter.
Your encouragement matters.
There is no price attached to the grace of God.
Jesus has already paid the cost of our redemption through His finished work.
Our desire is simply to make Him known.
And now, before you leave, return with me to the final scene of Judges.
The smoke has settled.
The armies are gone.
Families have been shattered.
The vulnerable have suffered.
The nation has survived, but it is deeply wounded.
And the writer leaves us with that haunting sentence:
“Every man did that which was right in his own eyes.”
For generations, humanity has repeated that tragedy in countless forms.
We have called pride strength.
We have called selfishness freedom.
We have called compromise wisdom.
We have called revenge justice.
We have called our preferences truth.
And we have sometimes called Jesus Lord while refusing to let Him rule.
But the Bible does not end in Judges.
The story moves forward.
Through the failures of kings.
Through the warnings of prophets.
Through exile, sorrow, and promises of restoration.
Until, in the fullness of time, a Child is born.
A Son is given.
And the King we could never produce through our own righteousness enters the world.
He touches the unclean.
He welcomes repentant sinners.
He confronts hypocrisy.
He defends the truth.
He goes to the cross.
He rises from the dead.
And He calls us to follow Him.
Not because we have always done what was right.
But because He alone is righteous.
Not because we deserve His kingdom.
But because His grace opens the way for sinners to be reconciled to God.
The final word over the believer is not self-rule.
It is the lordship of Jesus Christ.
And that is the hope we carry.
Not that human beings will finally become wise enough to save themselves.
But that the crucified and risen King is able to redeem those who turn to Him in faith.
So when you close this article, do not merely ask whether the ancient Israelites were wrong.
Ask whether Jesus truly has your heart.
Because you can win every argument, protect every excuse, and get everything you wanted—and still lose your way.
The most frightening place to be is not at the end of your strength, but at the center of your own throne, never realizing that the King who could save you is the One you keep refusing to obey.
